questions.q: Why does a production ServiceNow instance typically run across multiple application nodes?
options: For capacity and resilience — spreading incoming load so the platform can keep serving requests
Because a single node cannot store any customer data at all
Multiple nodes exist purely for cosmetic dashboard purposes
Nodes are only used in sub-production environments, never production
questions.explain: More nodes means more total capacity and the ability to keep serving requests even if one node needs attention.

questions.q: What does a semaphore actually limit?
options: How many forms can exist in the instance at once
The total number of users allowed to log in to the instance
How many requests of a certain category can execute simultaneously, per node
The maximum size of a single database table
questions.explain: Semaphores are a concurrency-control mechanism scoped to a category of work (such as background jobs), not a global limit on everything.

questions.q: Why does the platform give different categories of work their own separate semaphore pools?
options: So one category of work (like background processing) can't consume every available slot and starve other categories, like interactive transactions
ServiceNow requires separate pools for licensing reasons unrelated to performance
Every category of work actually shares one single unlimited pool today
Separate pools exist only to make the Instance Health dashboard look more detailed
questions.explain: Dividing node capacity deliberately by category protects each category from being starved by a saturated one.

questions.q: What happens when every slot in a semaphore's pool for a given category is currently busy?
options: All other categories of work are automatically paused too
Semaphore exhaustion — new requests of that same type must queue and wait for a slot to free up
The semaphore pool permanently doubles in size
The node immediately restarts itself
questions.explain: Exhaustion means the pool is full; new requests of that category wait their turn rather than running immediately.

questions.q: A request that would normally finish in under a second instead takes eight seconds, with semaphore exhaustion as the real cause. What does this tell you?
options: The request was waiting in queue for a slot, not inherently slow to process — the delay is resource contention, not request complexity
The instance's hardware has failed
Semaphore exhaustion has no effect on perceived request time at all
The underlying script is definitely broken and must be rewritten
questions.explain: This is the core diagnostic point of the lesson: queued-and-waiting looks identical to "slow" from the outside, but the fix targets contention, not the script.
